newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN BANKS - Reforms clean books, skirt big issues.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN BANKS - Reforms clean books, skirt big issues.

text.p: Financial sector reforms started in the early 1990s have tidied up the balance sheets of Indian public sector banks and improved operations, but a lot remains to be done if they are to measure up to global standards, bankers said.
"The first phase of banking reforms is over," said M.G. Bhide, chairman and managing director of Bank of India,BOI.BO, one of India's leading public sector banks.
"Bank balance sheets have been cleaned up and we are now in a better position to know where we stand," he said.
State-owned banks dominate India's banking industry with around 80 percent of all bank deposits and 78 percent of advances as of March 31, 1997 according to Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data.
Indian banking reforms were largely based on recommendations made by an expert group headed by former RBI governor M. Narasimham in 1991 to the finance ministry.

Many of the committee's recommendations have been implemented. The list includes the adoption of capital adequacy norms based on the Basle-based Bank for International Settlements, tougher norms for recognition of income, classification of loans, providing for bad loans and deregulation of interest rates.
The Narasimham committee also suggested a reduction in reserve requirements, which has also been implemented.

But other recommendations which are in cold storage include the setting up of special tribunals to speed up recovery of bank dues, merger of loss-making and smaller regional banks with bigger, profit-making ones and giving greater freedom to individual banks to recruit staff.
"The recommendations accepted so far are mostly accounting in nature," said K. Kannan, chairman and managing director of Bank of Baroda.
"The focus now will have to be on structural changes and more importantly on human resources," he said.
"I think the key lies in human resources...banks will have to be allowed to recruit the kind of people they need," he said.

Public sector banks at present have a common recruitment system, with staff being selected through a number of banking service recruitment boards across the country. The State Bank of India (SBI) and its seven fully-owned associates have separate recruitment boards.
The Narasimham panel had suggested dismantling of this system, saying: "This will provide scope for the banks to scout for talent and impart new skills to their personnel."

"Actually many of the reforms have got diluted because of the human resources (problem)," Kannan said. "If banks are to survive in a competitive environment, it will be possible only if they have the right staff."
"Otherwise we will still be in a situation where we are looking to the SBI (India's largest commercial bank) or Indian Banks' Association (IBA)," he said.
Kannan was referring to the deregulation of bank interest rates by the RBI after decades of central bank dictated-rates.
Most banks fought shy of charting up their own rates, and chose to wait for market leader SBI to announce its rates.
Other banks adopted interest rates on a consensus reached by the IBA, an association of Indian bank managements.
Bankers said critical areas of future reforms will include reduction of non-performing assets (NPAs) and debt recovery.
"Long-term viability (of banks) can be ensured only if NPAs are at lower levels," Bank of India's Bhide said.
The RBI has projected non-performing loans at 350.64 billion rupees or 13.55 percent of total bank advances of 2,588.61 billion rupees for the year ended March 31, 1997.

An expert group set up by the RBI to lay down a road-map for the rupee's capital account convertibility has said banks' non-performing loans should be brought down to 5.0 percent of total loans by 1999/2000.
It said this was the single most important factor determining the strength of the financial sector.
